nameStory: The 'bushy-backed' name comes from the elaborate, branching projections that sprout from this nudibranch's back, looking exactly like tiny underwater shrubs or bushes. The word 'frondosus' in its scientific name means 'leafy' in Latin, referring to these same decorative appendages that give it such a distinctive silhouette.
description: The bushy-backed nudibranch is a type of sea slug that looks like a living underwater garden ornament. These soft-bodied marine creatures are famous for their ornate, tree-like projections that branch off their backs in intricate patterns. They're typically translucent with delicate colors and can range from about half an inch to two inches long. As nudibranchs, they're shell-less relatives of snails that have evolved into some of the ocean's most beautiful and bizarre forms.

idTips.label: Branching back projections
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - elaborate, tree-like cerata (finger-like projections) that branch multiple times like tiny coral or fern fronds, feeling soft and almost jelly-like to the touch

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Body appears glass-like or semi-transparent, often with a pearlescent quality that seems to glow softly underwater

idTips.label: Prominent oral tentacles
idTips.description: Two horn-like tentacles at the front of the head that are often banded or ridged, used for detecting chemical signals in the water

idTips.label: Smooth gliding movement
idTips.description: Moves with a graceful, flowing motion across surfaces, leaving no visible slime trail like terrestrial slugs

idTips.label: Delicate coloration
idTips.description: Often displays subtle whites, pinks, or pale yellows with darker markings, colors may appear more vibrant when backlit

habitat: Look for bushy-backed nudibranchs in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal waters along New England's coast, particularly around Maine's colder waters. They're often found crawling on kelp, rockweed, or other seaweeds, and on the undersides of rocks in tide pools. These creatures prefer areas with good water circulation and are most commonly spotted during very low tides when their typical deeper haunts become accessible.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters begin to warm, often found in tide pools during extreme low tides. This is when they're easiest to spot as they move to shallower feeding areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation season when warm weather makes tide pooling most comfortable. Look during the lowest daytime tides when more of their habitat is exposed.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be found slightly deeper. Colors often appear more vibrant in the cooler, clearer water of early autumn.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen as they move to deeper waters and harsh conditions make tide pooling difficult. Occasional specimens may be found in protected, deeper tide pools.

funFact: Bushy-backed nudibranchs are solar-powered animals that steal chloroplasts from the algae they eat and incorporate them into their branching projections, allowing them to photosynthesize like plants and literally harvest energy from sunlight!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other branching nudibranchs, but the bushy-backed's projections branch multiple times like tiny trees, while similar species typically have simpler, unbranched finger-like projections. Memory trick: 'Bushy means branchy' - if the back projections look like miniature shrubs with multiple branches, you've found the right species.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills' in Latin, referring to their external breathing structures, though in this species the gills are actually hidden among all those decorative projections. Despite being called sea slugs, nudibranchs are actually more closely related to snails and represent one of evolution's most creative experiments in underwater beauty.
compareHints: The bushy-backed nudibranch differs from its relative the robust frond-aeolis mainly in the complexity of its branching - the bushy-backed has more elaborate, multiply-branched projections while the robust species tends to be bulkier with simpler branching patterns. The bushy-backed also tends to be more translucent and delicate-looking, while the robust frond-aeolis appears more solid and opaque.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the bushy-backed nudibranch in the same genus, the robust frond-aeolis lives up to its name with a notably thicker, more substantial body form.
